related_questions.question: What disease has the AAV vector cured in dogs?

text_blocks.snippet: In dogs, AAV (adeno-associated virus) vector-mediated gene therapy has shown promising results in treating hemophilia A and hemophilia B, two genetic bleeding disorders. Additionally, it has been explored for other conditions like Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) and glycogen storage disease type Ia (GSD-Ia).

list.title: Hemophilia:
list.snippet: AAV vectors have been used to deliver functional copies of the genes for clotting factors VIII (in hemophilia A) and IX (in hemophilia B) to the liver cells. This allows the liver to produce the missing clotting factors, effectively correcting the bleeding disorder.

list.title: Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy:
list.snippet: AAV vectors have been used to deliver a gene for a shortened version of the dystrophin protein (a mini-dystrophin) to muscle cells in dogs with DMD. This has shown promise in restoring some muscle function and reducing muscle damage.

list.title: Glycogen Storage Disease Type Ia:
list.snippet: AAV vectors have been used to deliver a functional gene for the enzyme glucose-6-phosphatase-α to liver cells in dogs with GSD-Ia. This has improved the survival and biochemical parameters of the affected dogs.

list.title: Sanfilippo syndrome:
list.snippet: Studies in mice and dogs with this lysosomal storage disease showed that gene therapy using an AAV vector can prevent neurodegeneration and improve behavior by delivering the missing enzyme to brain cells, according to the National Institutes of Health (NIH).

list.title: Long-term effects:
list.snippet: While AAV gene therapy has shown great promise, there are ongoing studies to assess the long-term safety and efficacy of the treatment, including the potential for long-term integration of the vector into the host's DNA and the development of immune responses.

text_blocks.snippet: Adeno-associated virus (AAV) itself is not known to cause any specific human disease. It is a small, non-enveloped virus that is replication-deficient, meaning it cannot replicate on its own and requires the presence of a helper virus (like adenovirus or herpesvirus) to complete its life cycle. While AAV can be found in humans, it is generally considered harmless and is often used as a vector in gene therapy.
snippet_highlighted_words: not known to cause any specific human disease

list.title: AAV is not pathogenic:
list.snippet: AAVs are not known to cause any disease in humans.

list.title: AAV needs a helper virus:
list.snippet: AAVs require the presence of a helper virus, like adenovirus or herpesvirus, to replicate.

list.title: AAV is used in gene therapy:
list.snippet: Due to its safety profile and ability to infect a wide range of cells, AAV is widely used as a vector for gene therapy.

list.title: AAV can be found in humans:
list.snippet: Serological studies have shown that many individuals have antibodies to AAV, indicating prior exposure.

list.title: AAV can integrate into the human genome:
list.snippet: AAV can integrate its DNA into the host cell's genome, but this is usually at a specific site and is considered relatively safe.

list.title: Potential concerns:
list.snippet: While AAV is generally considered safe, there are some potential concerns, such as insertional mutagenesis (where the AAV inserts its DNA in a way that disrupts a gene) and immune responses to the vector.

text_blocks.snippet: In summary, while AAV is not known to cause disease, its use in gene therapy requires careful consideration of potential risks, especially concerning immune responses and the possibility of insertional mutagenesis.
